issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise organized around war-zone trauma appraisals of injustice/accountability and a threat pattern of hypervigilance, startle, and concentration problems. Self-harm to release overwhelming feelings introduces a distinct affect-regulation strategy that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and sits poorly with the formulation, where Maladaptive Strategies has only a modest reciprocal link with Threat and no links from Negative Appraisals. Given the rest of the profile, a more threat-management strategy would be expected; this item feels clinically out of pattern rather than impossible.

vignette:
Kofi remembers the heat and the dust most clearly. It was his third tour with the relief agency, stationed at a food distribution point in a contested region. The work was grueling but felt meaningful. The moment it all changed began not with a bang, but with the squeal of tires from a pickup truck that careened around the corner of the makeshift market. For a split second, he registered the men in the back, the glint of metal, and then chaos erupted. The memory doesn't play like a film for him; it’s a series of frozen, blindingly bright snapshots. The overturned sacks of grain, the screams of the mothers he had been laughing with moments before, the feeling of being thrown against a wall. When he talks about it, which is rare, he describes it from a distance, as if narrating a scene he watched on a screen. This detachment is a skill he has honed; it feels like the only way to keep the images from swallowing him whole.

Back home in Chicago, the noise of the city became an enemy. The first time it happened, a car backfired on his street, and Kofi dropped to the floor of his living room before he even knew he was moving. His wife, Amara, found him crouched behind the sofa, heart hammering against his ribs. Since then, a constant, low-level hum of alertness has become his baseline. He is always scanning, always watchful. In his open-plan office, where he works as a social media manager, he can only sit at a desk that faces the entrance, his back firmly against a wall. He tracks everyone who comes and goes, his focus splintering with every new arrival. This state of being perpetually on guard has shredded his ability to concentrate. The vibrant, fast-paced digital world he once navigated with ease now feels like a minefield of overstimulation. He will stare at a screen for an hour, tasked with writing a cheerful caption for a client, but his mind is a blank slate, occupied only by the quiet, persistent task of monitoring his surroundings for any sign of threat.

The hardest part for Kofi is the gnawing sense of unfairness that churns in his gut. He follows the news from the region obsessively, searching for any mention of the attack, any report of arrests or accountability. There is never anything. The men in the truck simply vanished back into the chaos they created, and the world moved on. This lack of consequence has planted a deep and bitter root of injustice inside him. It feels personal, a confirmation that what happened to him, to the people he was trying to help, simply didn't matter. This feeling is tangled up with a profound loss of faith in himself. He replays the moment of the attack, convinced that he froze, that a better man would have done something—anything. This belief that he cannot rely on his own instincts has become a core truth. He questions every decision, from which route to take to the grocery store to how to respond to an email. He feels fundamentally broken, as if a critical component of himself was shattered in the dust that day and can never be recovered.

For months, he managed his internal world by simply refusing to engage with it. If a memory began to surface—the smell of diesel, the specific cry of a child—he would immediately get up, put on headphones with loud music, or lose himself in the meaningless scroll of his phone for hours. He avoided conversations about his work abroad and changed the channel if a news report felt too close to home. But the strategies are failing. Last month, his manager put him on a performance improvement plan, citing his missed deadlines and a sharp decline in the quality of his work. The conversation was the final straw. Staring at the sterile corporate document, Kofi felt the carefully constructed walls he had built around himself begin to crack. He came to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, terrified of losing his job and the life he has worked so hard to build, but even more afraid that the watchful, untrusting man he has become is all that is left of him.
